title: The depth of a module is at most dim(R/p) for every associated prime p
statement: Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be a Noetherian local ring [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring] (a Noetherian commutative ring with exactly one maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$) and let $M$ be a finite $R$-module [def-weil-finitely-generated-module]. Let $\mathfrak p\subset R$ be a prime ideal for which there is an element $z\in M$ with $\operatorname{Ann}_R(z)=\{a\in R: az=0\}=\mathfrak p$ (an associated prime of $M$). Then $\dim(R/\mathfrak p)\ge\operatorname{depth}(M)$, where $\dim(R/\mathfrak p)$ is the Krull dimension of the ring $R/\mathfrak p$ [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring] and $\operatorname{depth}(M)=\operatorname{depth}_{\mathfrak m}(M)$ is the depth [def-weil-pbc-depth].

proof.text: An associated prime makes M nonzero: in a subsingleton module no ideal is associated (Mathlib not_isAssociatedPrime_of_subsingleton). Nakayama implies m M != M. Unfold depth as the supremum of lengths of regular sequences in m.

proof.text: If m is associated, every x in m is a zerodivisor by the union-of-associated-primes characterization. The first member of any nonempty regular sequence would be regular, a contradiction. Every sequence contributing to depth is therefore empty, and the supremum is zero. Otherwise choose a regular x in m; the depth-drop theorem supplies a finite natural-number depth. Induct on d, uniformly over all nonzero finite R-modules of depth d and all their associated primes.

proof.text: For depth d+1, m cannot be associated by the zero-depth argument. Choose x in m regular on N; the zero-divisor characterization implies x not in p. Since p+(x) is contained in m, choose a prime q minimal over p+(x), contained in m. No maximal-dimension choice of q is required.

proof.text: The associated-prime power-quotient theorem gives n>=1 with q associated to Q=N/x^n N. The power x^n remains regular and in m. The depth-drop theorem gives Q nonzero and depth(Q)=d. Q is finite as a quotient, so induction gives d<=dim(R/q).

proof.text: The quotient factor map R/p onto R/q kills the image of x. This image is nonzero because x is outside p, hence a nonzerodivisor in the domain R/p. The inequality direction of the nonzerodivisor dimension-drop argument gives dim(R/q)+1<=dim(R/p): first quotient R/p by the image of x, then use monotonicity for the further quotient R/q. Lean uses Mathlib ringKrullDim_succ_le_of_surjective (Mathlib/RingTheory/KrullDimension/NonZeroDivisors.lean:61-65), which packages exactly these two inequalities, and does not require localness or finiteness. Adding one to the induction bound now gives d+1<=dim(R/p). This replaces the original equality and maximal-chain-attainment argument with only the inequality needed for induction.
